sections.title_en: 1. The Holiness of the Synagogue: the Survival of the Nation and Length of Days
sections.body_en:
A synagogue is a house that a community of Israel has established as a place of prayer to God, and by virtue of this God causes His Shekhina to dwell in it, and something like the holiness of the Temple is revealed in it; therefore it is called a 'small sanctuary' (mikdash me'at). And even while Israel are in exile, the Shekhina dwelt with them in hiddenness by means of the synagogues, in which faith in God and in the redemption of Israel was revealed. As the Sages said (Megilla 29a): "Come and see how beloved Israel are before the Holy One, blessed be He, for wherever they were exiled – the Shekhina is with them". As it is said (Yeḥezkel 11:16): "Thus says the Lord God: Although I have removed them far off among the nations, and although I have scattered them among the countries, yet I have been to them a small sanctuary in the countries where they have come". A small sanctuary – "these are the synagogues and the study halls".

Since the Shekhina dwells in a synagogue, whoever stays in it with seriousness fulfils a mitzva (Shulḥan Arukh 151:1, following Megilla 28b). Therefore, even one who has missed the minyan should preferably pray in a synagogue (Berakhot 6a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 90:9; Peninei Halakha, Prayer 3:1).

All the nations of the world, after they were exiled from their land, lost their identity within a few generations and ceased to exist. Only Israel, despite their long exile in the four corners of the earth, kept their identity. The synagogue has a great share in this, for the synagogue serves as a kind of spiritual extension drawn from the Temple and the Land of Israel, and every Jew who enters it, anywhere in the world, merits to connect to the holiness of the Land of Israel and to draw life from it. In this way, despite all the troubles and exiles, we were able to go on preserving our national identity, whose main expression is the belief that God is the Lord, and that Israel are destined to return to their land, to build the Temple and to bring blessing to the world (Megilla 29a. See Likkutei Halakhot, Beit Ha-Knesset 3). And if this is so outside the Land, how much more so do the synagogues in the Land of Israel draw illumination and great blessing from the Temple.

It is a mitzva for a person to fix for himself a place in which to pray in the synagogue (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 90:19). The Sages said (Berakhot 6b; 7b): "Whoever fixes a place for his prayer, the God of Avraham is his help", and "his enemies fall beneath him". Fixing the place expresses the fixed connection of the one praying to God, the source of life (Peninei Halakha, Prayer 3:2).

It is related in the Talmud (Berakhot 8a) that when Rabbi Yoḥanan heard that there were Jews in Babylonia who reached an extreme old age, he was very surprised and asked: but it is said (Devarim 11:21): "That your days may be multiplied, and the days of your children, upon the land which the Lord swore to your fathers to give them" – and not outside the Land. When they told him that those elders rose early to the synagogue in the morning and stayed late before leaving it in the evening, he said: this is what helped them to live long. For the holiness of the synagogue is akin to the holiness of the Land of Israel, the land of life (Kli Yakar, Devarim 11:21; Shela, Tamid, Ner Mitzva, gloss 2).

And likewise the Sages told of a woman in the Land of Israel who grew very old, until she became weary of her life. She came before Rabbi Yossi ben Ḥalafta and said to him: Rabbi, I have grown too old, and from now on it is a life of degradation, for I taste neither food nor drink, and I wish to depart from the world. He said to her: what mitzva are you accustomed to do every day? She said to him: I am accustomed, even if I have something dear to me, to leave it and rise early to the synagogue every day. He said to her: keep yourself from the synagogue for three consecutive days. She went and did so, and on the third day she fell ill and died. Concerning this Shlomo said (Mishlei 8:34-35): "Happy is the man who listens to me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at the posts of my doors. For whoever finds me finds life, and obtains favour from the Lord" (Yalkut Shimoni, Ekev 871).

A synagogue is a place in which the special quality of the unity of Israel is revealed, for it is intended for prayer with a minyan, that is, for the prayer of ten Jews who gather for this purpose, and therefore the Shekhina dwells among them. And since they are a minyan, they may say the devarim she-bi-kedusha: Kaddish and Barekhu, Kedusha and the repetition of the prayer leader, the Priestly Blessing and the Torah reading.

Since a synagogue expresses the unity of Israel, it must be open to every person of Israel. Similarly, the early authorities enacted that it is not within a person's authority, even if he was a partner in financing the building of the synagogue, to forbid another person by a vow to enter it (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 153:15).

Similarly, the poskim wrote that a ḥazan who intends not to fulfil the obligation of one of the worshippers – the other worshippers too do not fulfil their obligation (Rema, Oraḥ Ḥayim 581:1).

The early authorities further enacted that if a person lent his house to the community to serve as a synagogue, and he had a quarrel with one of the worshippers, he cannot forbid him to enter the synagogue. Rather, either he forbids the whole congregation together to enter his house, or he permits it to all of them (Shulḥan Arukh 153:16; Mishna Berura 88, and see Biur Halakha, s.v. 'Le-osrah'). However, if he is hosting them in his house, and it was not established that the room in which they pray is considered a synagogue at that time, he has the power to forbid one of the worshippers with whom he is in a quarrel to enter his house (Maharit Tzahalon 197; Peri Megadim, Eshel Avraham 39). And it seems that if that community has no other minyan, it is right for the congregation to pray in another house, so that that person can pray with a minyan (see Zera Emet part 1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 25, and Oraḥ Ne'eman 153:77, that if that person disturbs the congregation with quarrels, the owner of the house may forbid him to enter his house).

The prayer said in the synagogue also expresses the unity of Israel, for the essence of communal prayer is for the whole of Israel, and from within this each individual asks his particular requests. In order to highlight this principle, the holy Ari urged his students to take upon themselves before prayer to fulfil the mitzva of "you shall love your neighbour as yourself" (Sha'ar Ha-Kavanot of the Ari). And so the poskim wrote (Ḥayei Adam 1:6): "He should take upon himself specifically to love each and every person as himself, as it is said (Vayikra 19:18): You shall love your neighbour as yourself. And through this he will include his prayer in the general prayers of all Israel, and they will become one" (and so in the Magen Avraham 46, introduction; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 11; the Ḥida).

As an expression of love and unity, Israel are accustomed that when one of the worshippers has a joyous occasion, such as a bar mitzva, a birth or a wedding – he is called up to the Torah and the gabbai adds a blessing for him, and all the worshippers answer 'Amen' to the blessing and share in his joy. Likewise, people are accustomed that the gabbai blesses those called up to the Torah, and when they return to their places their neighbours shake their hands and say to them 'Yishar koaḥ' or 'Ḥazak u-varukh'. And people are likewise accustomed to bless and thank the ḥazanim after they have led the prayer. And likewise, may it not befall us, when a person is mourning one of his family members, they comfort him, and honour him to say Kaddish for the elevation of the soul of his relative, and the whole congregation answers 'Amen' after the Kaddish.

As an expression of love of Israel, although it is a mitzva to pray in a fixed place in the synagogue (Peninei Halakha, Prayer 3:2), when a guest sits down in a worshipper's fixed place, it is preferable for the owner of the place to sit somewhere else and avoid causing him distress.

sections.title_en: 3. The Holiness of a Synagogue, and How It Becomes Sanctified
sections.body_en:
A synagogue is a holy place, and one must conduct oneself in it with awe, for it is said concerning the Temple: "and you shall revere My sanctuary" (Vayikra 19:30), and the holiness of a synagogue, which is called a 'small sanctuary', is akin to the holiness of the Temple. Some say that the holiness of the synagogue is from the Torah, that is, that the mitzva to build a synagogue is a branch of the mitzva to build the Temple, and therefore its holiness is akin to the holiness of the Temple (Yere'im). And the view of most poskim is that from the Torah the mitzva is to establish the Temple, and it was the Sages who established a mitzva of their own to establish a synagogue for every community, in order to extend the holiness of the Temple to all the communities of Israel, and therefore the holiness of the synagogue is rabbinic. But it seems that even according to their view, since a synagogue is a place set aside for the service of God, one who treats it with disrespect negates the mitzva of the fear of God, as it is said (Devarim 10:20): "You shall fear the Lord your God".1

In order for a certain house to be considered a synagogue, two conditions must be fulfilled in it: first, that the intention of its owners is to designate it as a synagogue; second, that people actually begin to pray in it. Therefore, while the synagogue is being built, the laws of its holiness do not yet apply to it, and it is permitted to play in it. And only from the moment they began to pray in it – do all the laws of a synagogue apply to it (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 153:8).

A community that has not yet built itself a synagogue, and in the meantime its members pray on Shabbatot and festivals in a building intended for another purpose, such as the hall of the local school – the laws of a synagogue do not apply to the hall, since it was not designated for this. Therefore, outside the prayer times it is permitted to play and exercise in it. And likewise a hall intended for the activities of a youth movement, in which the youngsters are accustomed to pray on Shabbat – since that hall was not designated as a synagogue, it is permitted to hold activities and performances in it and to laugh in it (Megilla 26a; Shulḥan Arukh 154:1). But one must set up a partition such as a curtain between the Holy Ark and the rest of the hall. First, in order to emphasise that the hall was indeed not designated as a synagogue. Second, because it is forbidden to act with levity in front of the Torah scroll, and even in front of the Holy Ark with the Torah scroll inside it (see Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 282:1; Mishna Berura 150:14, and Sha'ar Ha-Tziyun 13).

Those who rent a place to serve them as a synagogue: if it is in a temporary manner and they do not furnish it as a synagogue, it does not have the law of a synagogue. And if they furnish it as a synagogue, one must treat it with the holiness of a synagogue for the whole period of the rental, unless they stipulated that the holiness of a synagogue would not apply to it during the rental (see Shulḥan Arukh 154:2; Mishna Berura 5; Biur Halakha there; Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 14-15).

notes_en.en: According to the Yere'im (104), the holiness of the synagogue is from the Torah, for "just as it is forbidden to benefit from consecrated property – so it is forbidden to benefit from synagogues and study halls that were set aside for prayer and for expounding, for this too is consecrated property". And so he wrote there 409: "'And you shall fear your God' – he commanded that when a person enters the Temple or the synagogue or the study hall, he should conduct himself in them with reverence and honour, as it is written in parashat Behar Sinai: You shall keep My Shabbatot and revere My sanctuary – you are not to revere the sanctuary, but the One who warned concerning the sanctuary, meaning: the Holy One, blessed be He. And we find that the synagogue and the study hall are called 'sanctuary', as it is taught in Torat Kohanim: And I will bring your sanctuaries to desolation – sanctuary, My sanctuaries, your sanctuaries – to include synagogues and study halls". We have learned that synagogues and study halls are included in the Torah mitzva 'revere My sanctuary'. And so wrote Ḥayei Adam (17:6) and the Ben Ish Ḥai (Vayikra 1). On the other hand, according to the Ran, the holiness of the synagogue is rabbinic, and so it follows from the Ramban, the Ritva and the Rashba. And so wrote most Aḥaronim, among them: the Peri Megadim (Mishbetzot Zahav 151:1), Divrei Ḥayim (1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 3), Beit Shlomo (Oraḥ Ḥayim 28), Torat Ḥesed (Oraḥ Ḥayim 4:7), the Maharshag (2:38), Mikveh Ha-Mayim (4, Oraḥ Ḥayim 19), and others. And see the Sedei Ḥemed (Kelalim, ma'arekhet bet 43). And in Responsa Beit Yitzḥak (Even Ha-Ezer 2:33) he wrote that even according to those who hold that the holiness of the synagogue is rabbinic, the prohibition against treating it with disrespect is from the Torah. Similar to what the Rivash (220) wrote: although a sage who waived his honour – his honour is waived, he cannot waive his being disgraced. Until here. Since according to the majority of poskim the holiness of the synagogue is rabbinic, in a situation of doubt – the halakha is lenient (R. Ḥayim David, Mayim Ḥayim 2:19).

sections.body_en:
The synagogue is designated for sacred matters, for prayer and for Torah, and whoever uses it for secular purposes or treats it in a secular manner degrades its holiness. Therefore, one does not behave in it with levity through joking and jesting, and one does not eat and drink in it, and one does not speak in it about secular matters such as trade and economics, and one does not read secular messages on the phone in it. Likewise, it is forbidden to read newspapers in it or to browse news sites on the internet, and this includes religious newspapers and sites (Megilla 28a-b; Shulḥan Arukh 151:1).

When a person comes in to pray he must make sure that the phone does not distract him from the prayer, and does not draw him into engaging in secular matters in the synagogue. Therefore he should put it in his pocket or his bag, and silence it so that it does not disturb him when messages and notifications arrive. Likewise, it is preferable that a person not pray from the phone, so that his mind will not be distracted by it to other matters. But when necessary he may pray from the phone while blocking messages. A person who is required to be available for security needs, or to provide urgent medical help, or for another important need, should set the phone so that it alerts him only to urgent messages.

The Sages said that one who treats the synagogue with disrespect causes separation between Israel and God, for the Shekhina is revealed in the synagogue, whereas he ignores this and degrades the synagogue with idle matters; he has no share in the God of Israel, and he diminishes faith, so that it is not revealed in the place fitting for it (see Zohar part 2, 131b).

It is a mitzva to honour the synagogue and to see to its cleanliness, and one who has mud on his shoes must clean them before he enters the synagogue. Likewise, it is fitting not to enter the synagogue in dirty clothes (Shulḥan Arukh 151:8-9). One who unwittingly came into the synagogue with mud must clean what he dirtied, in order to repair the damage he did to the honour of the synagogue, and so as not to continue to distress those who come to the synagogue. And if the one who made the dirt was negligent and did not clean it, it is a mitzva for anyone who can to honour the synagogue and clean up the mud. And it is a kal va-ḥomer: if in a private house the members of the household are usually careful not to dirty its floor with mud, and if one of the household saw that it had become dirty and is able to clean it, it is expected that he will clean it and not leave the house in its dirt – how much more so must one act so in a synagogue, which it is a mitzva to honour.

Likewise, it is forbidden to leave on the tables of the synagogue or the study hall tissues with which dirt was cleaned or a nose was wiped.

One who needs to blow his nose, cough or clear his throat should do so politely, while trying not to make more noise than is necessary, for otherwise he would be affronting the honour of the synagogue and the honour of the congregation.

It is forbidden to spit in the synagogue. True, there were times when people were accustomed to spit in houses whose floors were of stone, brick or earth, and therefore when necessary they were lenient about this in the synagogue too (Shulḥan Arukh 151:7). But today, when it is shameful to spit in a house, all the more so it is forbidden to spit in the synagogue.

The Sages said (Megilla 28b): "One does not beautify oneself in them and one does not stroll in them". The meaning of 'one does not beautify oneself' is that it is forbidden to adorn oneself in the synagogue. Included in this, it is forbidden for a man to shave in the synagogue and forbidden for a woman to put on make-up in it. And likewise it is forbidden to have a haircut in the synagogue, and even the start of the haircut of a three-year-old (ḥalaka) may not be done in the synagogue (Lev Ḥayim 2:172; Sedei Ḥemed). Some are lenient about this, since they consider it a mitzva custom (Shulḥan Gavoha 531:13). But from the outset it is right to be stringent about this.

Included in 'one does not beautify oneself', one does not sit in the synagogue the way a person usually sits at home freely, leaning back in the manner of reclining, or stretching out one's legs in a disrespectful way. Rather, one should sit in the synagogue respectfully, as befits one who is in a holy place (Me'iri, Megilla 28b; Olat Tamid 151:1).

'One does not stroll' means that a person is forbidden to stroll back and forth in the synagogue for his pleasure, and likewise one does not sit idly in it (Shulḥan Arukh 151:1).

In addition to the custom that Israel adopted of wearing a kippa, there is an obligation to cover the head while in the synagogue (Shulḥan Arukh 151:6; 91:3; above 5:2, note 2). Likewise, married women have a double obligation to cover their heads in the synagogue (see Peninei Halakha, Women's Prayer 10:6, note 6). A non-Jew who visits the synagogue must also cover his head (and see Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 13:11).

Many ruled that a person is forbidden to kiss his children in the synagogue and to show them extra affection, in order to fix in his heart that there is no love like the love of the Omnipresent (Rema 98:1). In addition, one must take care not to bring to the synagogue at prayer time small children who do not know how to sit respectfully, because they are liable to degrade the honour of the synagogue and to disturb the concentration of the worshippers (Shela; Mishna Berura 98:3; Peninei Halakha, Prayer 5:6). However, it is permitted to kiss the hands of the rabbi, because this is not a kiss of love but of honour for the Torah. And likewise it is permitted to kiss the hands of one's father after he has been called up to the Torah, for this kiss too is for the sake of honour (Ben Ish Ḥai, Vayikra 11). And likewise it is permitted to kiss the hands of relatives whom one is obligated to honour, such as an older brother or a father-in-law (Kitzur Shulḥan Arukh of Toledano 27:4). And many of the immigrants from North Africa were accustomed to kiss each other on the face in the synagogue as a sign of friendship and love, and although there were some among the rabbis of Morocco who preferred to abolish their custom, since they were accustomed so with the agreement of rabbis, those who wish to continue their custom may do so.2

It is forbidden to smoke in the synagogue. True, in the past, just as they permitted Torah learners to eat in the study hall in order to prevent neglect of Torah study, so they were accustomed to permit smoking to someone who found it difficult to study without it. But after it was discovered that smoking harms health, it is forbidden to smoke anywhere, because smoking harms the smoker and those around him, and all the more so it is forbidden to smoke in a holy place.

Several of the sages of the Rishonim wrote that it is forbidden to enter the synagogue with a long knife, because prayer lengthens a person's life, whereas the sword and the knife shorten life (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 151:6). Similarly, the Sages said that one should not enter the study hall with a spear (Sanhedrin 82a). And the same is the law concerning a pistol and a rifle, that one should not enter the synagogue and the study hall with them. However, when it concerns police officers or soldiers whose task is to protect security, their weapons do not express the shortening of life but the protection of life. All the more so at a time when there is a security need for people to carry weapons in order to protect against terrorists, it is a mitzva for anyone who contributes to security to have weapons with him in the synagogue and the study hall. But people who are not charged with security, at a time when there is no security need, should not enter the synagogue with weapons. And if they have weapons on them and there is danger in leaving them outside the synagogue, they may enter the synagogue with them, while making an effort to conceal them.3

notes_en.en:
Responsa Binyamin Ze'ev (163, in the name of the Agudah) and Sefer Ḥasidim (255) wrote that a person should not kiss his children in the synagogue, "to make known that there is no love like the love of the Holy One, blessed be He", and they did not distinguish between small and grown children. And so Rav Kook inferred (Oraḥ Mishpat, Oraḥ Ḥayim 22), that grown children too should not be kissed. However, the Rema (Oraḥ Ḥayim 98:1) and the Ben Ish Ḥai (Vayikra 11) wrote that a person is forbidden to kiss his small children in the synagogue, and Rav Yosef Mashash explained (Otzar Ha-Mikhtavim 3:1787) that the prohibition is to kiss and hug children out of love, but it is permitted to kiss adult relatives, for this is a kiss for the sake of honour, and especially to kiss one who has been called up to the Torah, which is for the honour of the Torah.
Many of the immigrants from North Africa were accustomed to kiss each other's faces in the synagogue as a sign of friendship and love; however, Rav Ḥazan of Morocco wrote (Yeḥaveh Da'at 3, Oraḥ Ḥayim 5) that this custom, which arose anew in the large cities of Morocco, should not be kept, for people were not accustomed so in the past. And only one whom a person is obligated to honour, or a Torah scholar, may be kissed. And so wrote Rav Maman (Emek Yehoshua 3, Oraḥ Ḥayim 18; 6, Oraḥ Ḥayim 21). However, Rav Shalom Mashash wrote (Shemesh U-Magen 1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 39) that a kiss between friends and relatives is in the category of "a greeting and an expression of affection and friendship, and there is no diminishing of love for God, Heaven forbid, in this", and it is for the honour of the Torah, and he explained that Rav Kook too would agree to this.

The Tashbetz (202) and Orḥot Ḥayim (Laws of the Synagogue 7) wrote, in the name of the Maharam of Rothenburg, that one should not enter the synagogue with a long knife. The Shulḥan Arukh (151:6) brought this view. And Rabbeinu Peretz wrote (glosses on the Tashbetz Katan, and Kolbo 17) that if the knife is covered – it is permitted, and so wrote many Aḥaronim (Eliya Rabba 151:10; Mor U-Ketzi'a; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 10, and others). As for the entry of police officers and soldiers, since they are charged with security – their weapons do not express the shortening of days. Rav Shmuel David wrote along these lines (Me-Rosh Tzurim 8), and see the Tzitz Eliezer (10:18) and Terumat Ha-Goren (1:35).

sections.title_en: 6. Not to Enter the Synagogue for a Secular Purpose
sections.body_en:
The synagogue is designated for sacred matters, therefore one enters the synagogue only for a mitzva purpose (Rambam, Laws of Prayer 11:8), and whoever enters it for another purpose affronts its honour. Therefore, it is forbidden to enter the synagogue in order to shelter from rain or from heat, or in order to arrange a meeting with a friend, or in order to use a socket in it to charge one's phone or computer.

However, when necessary the Sages permitted a person to enter the synagogue for a personal need, on condition that beforehand he honours it by some study. Therefore, one who needs to call his friend out of the synagogue should go in and study one halakha or one verse, and only afterwards call his friend. And if he does not know how to study, he should stay a little in silence and respectfully, because staying in the synagogue respectfully is also a mitzva (Megilla 28b; Shulḥan Arukh 151:1). Similarly, when it rains, when necessary it is permitted to enter the synagogue with the intention of studying a little in it. And from the outset he should study for the whole time that he stays in it.4

A synagogue that has two entrances – one should not make it a short cut (kapandarya), that is, one should not enter by one entrance and leave by the other in order to shorten one's way. And even if he is going for a mitzva purpose he should not do so (Megilla 29a; Shulḥan Arukh 151:5; Biur Halakha, s.v. 'Le-katzer'). However, when necessary, if he stays in the synagogue and studies one halakha or one verse, he may shorten his way through it. And one who entered the synagogue in order to pray or study – it is an enhancement that he leave by the other entrance, even when he thereby shortens his way. For in this way he merits to linger in both sides of the synagogue and passes through both its entrances, and thereby expresses the endearment of the synagogue (Levush; Mishna Berura 151:21). In the courtyard of the synagogue and the corridor leading to it, there is no prohibition against passing through as a short cut (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 151:8).5

It is permitted to enter the synagogue in order to look at its beauty and its splendour, because such a stay in the synagogue also honours it and is considered a mitzva, all the more so when one also learns about the community or its rabbis. However, it is forbidden to enter the synagogue in order to learn about its architecture (see Leket Ha-Kemaḥ He-Ḥadash 151:30). And if they study a little in it – it is permitted.

notes_en.en: According to the Mishna Berura (151:4), even if he honours the synagogue with a brief study, it is forbidden to enter because of the rain, because he can enter another place, and so wrote Az Nidberu (8:51). However, from several Rishonim it follows that if he honours the synagogue with a brief study he may enter even because of the rain (Ra'avya, Megilla 591; Semag, positive commandments 19; Tosafot of the Sages of England). And so wrote in practice the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (151:4), Seridei Esh (part 2, 12:5), and Me'or Yisrael of Rav Ovadia Yosef (Megilla there).

The Sages forbade shortening one's way through a synagogue that has two entrances; however, when one entered in order to pray or study, it is permitted to shorten one's way by leaving through the other entrance (Megilla 29a). And so wrote the Rambam (Laws of Prayer 11:10) and the Shulḥan Arukh (151:5). And some read that it is a 'mitzva' to leave through the other entrance (Behag, Rosh, Tur, and others), as the pilgrims did when they came to the Temple (as explained in Yeḥezkel 46:9). The Ran explained (there 9b, in the Rif's pages): "because he appears to hold it dear". And in the Levush (151:5): "When they enter by this entrance and leave by another entrance, everyone will be seen in all sides of the court of the synagogue, that they all gathered to bow down in the house of God and to pray before Him, may He be blessed, and this is for His glory and honour, may He be blessed". And so wrote in practice the Magen Avraham 7, Mekor Ḥayim of the Ḥavot Ya'ir, Eliya Rabba 9, the Mishna Berura 21, the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 8 and the Ben Ish Ḥai, Vayikra 9.
Some say that only one who entered in order to pray or study has a mitzva to leave by another entrance, but he is forbidden to shorten his way on the basis of saying a verse or a halakha (Or Same'aḥ, Laws of Prayer 11:10; Halikhot Shlomo 19:2; Halikhot Olam, Vayikra 5). And some hold that if he says a verse there is no mitzva in it, but he may shorten his way (Kolbo 17; Biur Halakha, s.v. 'La-asoto'; Ben Ish Ḥai there). And this is what I wrote above for when it is necessary, on condition that he studies a verse or a halakha and does not merely recite it as if discharging a duty.
When the path preceded the synagogue, it is permitted to make it a short cut (Megilla 29a), and so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (151:5), and Oraḥ Ne'eman (151:19) reinforced his ruling. However, Rabbi Avraham Min Ha-Har learned from the Rif and the Rambam that the halakha is not so. And so wrote Nimukei Maharai (Laws of Prayer 11:8). And according to many Rishonim, it is permitted to shorten one's way when the path came first, but it is a pious custom to be stringent in this, as Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua did (Megilla 27b; Rashba, Tosafot Ha-Rosh, Ritva, Me'iri, Turei Even. And according to the Eliya Rabba 151:8 this is how it is fitting to act). If people were accustomed to pass through the entrance hall to the study rooms adjacent to the synagogue, and they turned the entrance hall into a room in which people also pray, or into a women's section, it is permitted to pass through it for the purpose of study, for this too is an example of a path that preceded the synagogue (Tzitz Eliezer 12:16; Halikhot Shlomo 19:3).

sections.body_en:
Synagogues and study halls are intended for prayer and Torah, and therefore one should not eat and drink in them, and one should not sleep in them. However, when there is a need, in order to prevent neglect of Torah study, it is permitted to eat and drink in the study hall. For since the purpose of study halls is to increase Torah, when necessary it is preferable to give up a little in preserving their honour in order to add time for Torah study. Therefore, if in order to eat and drink the learners would have to go home and lose study time, they were lenient that they may eat and drink in them, while taking care about cleanliness. And the same is the law of a synagogue in which people are accustomed to study, at the time of study (Shulḥan Arukh 151:1; Magen Avraham 2).

But in yeshivot, in which the dining room is near the study hall, one should not eat in it, because there is no need for it. Likewise, in study halls in which avrekhim study, if they have a room in which they can eat, they should not eat in the study hall. However, drinking water, tea and coffee – is permitted, in order to prevent neglect of Torah study. And some also need to taste something while studying, and it is permitted to them in order to prevent neglect of Torah study, while taking care about cleanliness.

Similarly, in a pressing situation Torah learners are permitted to speak a little in the study hall about secular matters and necessary business, so that they will not need to leave the study hall and interrupt their study (Misgeret Ha-Shulḥan 13:1). Included in this, it is permitted to look at the phone if messages have arrived that require an urgent answer. If the looking and the answer are short – they may be done in the study hall, and if they become lengthy – one must leave the study hall.

And likewise concerning sleep. From the outset one should not sleep or even doze in the study hall, and the Sages said (Sanhedrin 71a): "Whoever sleeps in the study hall – his Torah becomes torn to shreds". However, when necessary, in order to prevent neglect of Torah study, they permitted one who studies in the study hall and feels tired to sleep in a temporary way, that is, to lay his head on the table or the shtender and sleep a little, in order to return to study with renewed strength (Shulḥan Arukh 151:3). In a pressing situation, they permitted a Torah scholar who studies regularly in the study hall day and night to sleep in the study hall at night even a fixed sleep (Levush; Mishna Berura 16). However, those who are meticulous refrain from this, and it is related (Megilla 28a) that one of the reasons by virtue of which Rabbi Zeira lived long was that he did not sleep in the study hall, neither a fixed sleep nor even a temporary sleep.6

notes_en.en:
Megilla (28a-b): "The Rabbis taught: Synagogues – one does not behave in them with levity: one does not eat in them, nor drink in them, nor beautify oneself in them, nor stroll in them… Rava said: Sages and their students are permitted. For Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: What is 'bei rabbanan'? The house of the Rabbis". According to the Rambam (Laws of Prayer 11:6), Orḥot Ḥayim and the Me'iri, the permission for a Torah scholar to eat, drink and sleep in the study hall is under pressure, in order to prevent neglect of Torah study, and so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (151:1). And according to the Rashba and the Ran, the permission applies even not under pressure: although a study hall is holier than a synagogue, since it is like the house of a Torah scholar, they permitted him to eat and sleep in it; and so wrote the Rema there. And so it follows from many Rishonim who brought the Gemara that the study hall is considered the house of Torah scholars, without qualifying that the permission is only under pressure (Rabbeinu Ḥananel, the Rif, Or Zarua, Ra'avya, Rid, Riaz, Rosh, Semak. And so Rabbi Avraham Min Ha-Har explained this view). And some decided so in halakha (Baḥ 2; Knesset Ha-Gedola, Hagahot Beit Yosef 1).
However, the Magen Avraham (151:2) brought the views closer, and wrote that the permission of the lenient views is only for one who studies regularly, who may eat and drink while he studies in order to prevent neglect of Torah study. And in this both the Rambam and the Ran can agree (Maḥatzit Ha-Shekel). Similarly, the Perisha (151:3) wrote according to the lenient view that the leniency is because the eating and drinking are for the sake of the study, in order to prevent neglect of Torah study. And so wrote the Mishna Berura 7 and Sha'ar Ha-Tziyun 12.
Above I wrote that a synagogue in which people are accustomed to study has the law of a study hall at the time of study. So wrote R. Shmuel Aboab (Devar Shmuel 346). And the Be'er Heitev (153:2) and Magen Gibborim (there 2) explained that even a fixed hour a day makes it considered a study hall. And so wrote Rav Zirelson (Atzei Levanon, Oraḥ Ḥayim 5) and Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach (Halikhot Shlomo 5:3).

sections.body_en:
When necessary it is permitted to hold a mitzva meal in the synagogue and the study hall, for it is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud (Pesaḥim 1:1) that when the rabbis gathered in the synagogue for the sanctification of the month they would hold a meal (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 151:4). Similarly, people are accustomed to hold a brit mila in the synagogue and to drink wine from the cup of blessing, since this is a mitzva.

Some say that only a small mitzva meal was permitted to be held in the synagogue when necessary, for at the sanctification of the month and the intercalation of the year they ate bread and legumes. Included in this, it is also permitted to serve light refreshments, as is customary on a yahrzeit. But a large meal at which much alcoholic drink is drunk is forbidden; therefore it is forbidden to hold in a synagogue the meal of a brit mila, sheva berakhot or a siyum of a tractate (Magen Avraham 151:5; Eliya Rabba 7; Peri Megadim; Ben Ish Ḥai, Vayikra 4). On the other hand, some say that when necessary it is permitted to hold in a synagogue even a mitzva meal at which much alcoholic drink is drunk, on condition that they preserve the holiness of the place and do not become drunk. And as people were accustomed, when necessary, to hold Kiddush and Shabbat meals in the synagogue for poor guests.

In practice, in a place where people are accustomed to hold se'uda shelishit in the synagogue, they may continue their custom. And likewise, in a place where people usually hold the meals of a brit mila and pidyon ha-ben in the synagogue, it is permitted to hold any mitzva meal, including a bar mitzva meal and sheva berakhot. This is on condition that they take care to preserve the holiness of the synagogue, and avoid idle talk and levity. And likewise they should take care to avoid mixing of men and women. But in a place where people were not accustomed to hold mitzva meals in the synagogue, it is preferable to follow the stringent view not to hold large mitzva meals in it. And those who wish to be lenient may rely on the many poskim who were lenient about this, especially when there is an educational benefit in it.7

notes_en.en:
It is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud (Pesaḥim 1:1; Sanhedrin 8:2) that they ate Shabbat meals and the meal of the sanctification of the month in the synagogue and the study hall. And likewise it is brought in the Babylonian Talmud (Pesaḥim 100b) that there were guests who ate and slept in the synagogue, and they would make Havdala over a cup of wine in the synagogue. The Rishonim raised a difficulty from Megilla (28a), where it is explained that it is forbidden to eat in the synagogue! And they gave three explanations: a) the guests did not eat in the synagogue but in the rooms adjoining it (Rashba 4:278; Mordekhai, Pesaḥim 611; Rosh, Bava Batra 1:4. And so wrote the Geonim, Tosafot and many other Rishonim in one of their explanations). b) it is permitted to eat a mitzva meal such as a Shabbat meal in the synagogue (Semag, positive commandments 29; Semak, Orḥot Ḥayim, Nimukei Yosef. And so it is brought in the Geonim, Tosafot, the Ran and many other Rishonim in one of the explanations). c) the permission is because the synagogues in Babylonia were built on condition that if needed it would be permitted to host guests in them or to use them for communal needs (Ra'avya 2:509; Rashba there; Rav Kafiḥ in his explanation of the Rambam, Laws of Shabbat 29:8, note 25). In the Shulḥan Arukh (151:4) it was ruled that it is permitted to eat and sleep in the synagogue itself for the needs of the synagogue, such as to guard the lamps. And likewise it is permitted to hold mitzva meals, such as the meal of the intercalation of the year.
Some say that a mitzva meal is permitted on condition that it is small, such as the meal of the intercalation of the year, which was held with bread and legumes and in which there was no concern of drunkenness (Magen Avraham 151:5; Eliya Rabba 7; Peri Megadim, Eshel Avraham there; Sho'el U-Meshiv, sixth edition 3; Ben Ish Ḥai, Vayikra 4; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 151:6; Har Tzvi, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:73). And some say that a mitzva meal is permitted even if it is large, and that people were accustomed so to hold in the synagogue also the meals of a brit mila and a siyum of a tractate (Keren Le-David, Oraḥ Ḥayim 37; Torat Ḥayim 151:9; Benei Tziyon of Lichtman 151:4; 269:3; Seridei Esh part 1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 16:19). And likewise people were accustomed to eat se'uda shelishit in the synagogue with drink (Yabi'a Omer part 10, Oraḥ Ḥayim 14; see Or Le-Tziyon part 2, 10:4). However, one must take care that they do not come to levity and mixing of men and women (Mor U-Ketzi'a), or to drunkenness (Tzitz Eliezer 14:26:2). In Ḥasidic communities people were accustomed to be more lenient, and they considered the synagogues and study halls as the house of the Rebbe, or as the house of the Ḥasidim, and therefore it does not have the law of a synagogue (following Divrei Ḥayim, Ḥoshen Mishpat 2:32).
In addition, in places where everyone was accustomed to be lenient to hold certain mitzva meals in a synagogue, it is possible that even according to the stringent view they may be lenient, for they are considered as having stipulated so from the beginning, and some say that the stipulation helps (see Mishna Berura 151:5; Sha'ar Ha-Tziyun 4; Biur Halakha 151:11, s.v. 'Aval be-yishuvo', 'Aval be-vatei knesiyot'; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 5), and in a place where this is the custom one may rely on them.
A stipulation: Megilla 28b: "Rabbi Asi said: The synagogues in Babylonia are made on condition, and even so one does not behave in them with levity. And what is that? Calculations". According to Rashi, the Or Zarua (2:388), the Nimukei Yosef and R. Avraham Min Ha-Har, the stipulation permits making secular uses of the synagogue even while it is standing, but not things involving levity. And according to the Ramban, the Rashba and the Ran, the stipulation helps while it is standing only for communal needs, according to the time and the matter. Whereas according to Tosafot (Megilla 28b, s.v. 'Batei knesiyot') and the Rosh (4:7), the stipulation helps only after its destruction, when it will be permitted to make secular uses of it that involve no disrespect, and so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (151:11). (As for calculations, according to Tosafot they are permitted after its destruction, and according to the Rosh they involve disrespect and are therefore forbidden even after its destruction.) According to Tosafot and the Shulḥan Arukh a stipulation helps only outside the Land, as in Babylonia, because the holiness of the synagogues there is destined to lapse, and not in the Land of Israel. However, the Eliya Rabba (17) and the Biur Halakha (there, s.v. 'Batei knesiyot') wrote that from all the other Rishonim it is implied that the stipulation helps in the Land of Israel too.
Some say that in order to permit secular uses it is right to make an explicit stipulation (Magen Avraham 151:12; Ḥatam Sofer 1:30). And some say that when the prevalent custom is to be lenient, it is considered as though they stipulated (Rema 154:8; Eliya Rabba 151:17). And so is the custom; see below 14:7.
It seems that for those who are accustomed to be lenient to hold large meals in the synagogue, during the meal a person may speak a little with his neighbour, in friendship and respect, about secular matters, such as hearing what he does at work and whether he bought a new house, even though at another time these conversations are forbidden in the synagogue. This is because this is what is customary at a meal, and there is no additional affront to the honour of the synagogue beyond the affront in holding the meal itself. And they must refrain only from conversations about idle matters and levity.

sections.body_en:
Although people are accustomed to hold a brit mila in the synagogue, many refrain from holding a ḥuppa in it, since a large crowd takes part in it, and it is difficult to preserve the seriousness and modesty required in the synagogue.

And some are accustomed to hold a ḥuppa in the synagogue while taking care to separate men and women, as is customary in a synagogue, but the meal is not held in the synagogue, since people usually rejoice at it with excessive and unrestrained joy. And when necessary, when the crowd numbers a few dozen, some are accustomed to be lenient to hold the wedding meal too in the synagogue, while taking care about the rules of honour and modesty.8

notes_en.en: In the past some in Ashkenaz were accustomed to hold the ḥuppot in the synagogue (see Rema, Yoreh De'ah 391:3; Beit Shmuel 30:9). However, later many of those of Ashkenazi origin were accustomed to hold the ḥuppa under the open sky, and so the custom of holding ḥuppot in the synagogue lapsed (Mas'at Binyamin 109; Ḥatam Sofer, Even Ha-Ezer 98). Not only that, but some say that since people became accustomed not to hold ḥuppot in the synagogue, it is forbidden to hold them in it (Imrei Esh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 10; Sho'el U-Meshiv, third edition 1:182; see Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 28:9). But among those of Sephardi origin and some of those of Ashkenazi origin, some are accustomed to hold ḥuppot in the synagogue (Nehar Mitzrayim, Kiddushin 14). But the wedding meal, which by its nature involves unrestrained joy, should not be held in the synagogue. But if in practice the number of participants in the meal is small, its law is like that of a sheva berakhot meal and a brit mila, and then in a synagogue where people are accustomed to be lenient to hold those, it is permitted to hold a quiet wedding meal.

sections.body_en:
A synagogue and a study hall are intended for sacred matters, and therefore it is forbidden to talk in them about money and business. And even a community that needs to hold a meeting on matters of money and organisation, and has no suitable place to hold it other than the synagogue, should not hold it there, out of respect for the synagogue (Biur Halakha 151:1, s.v. 'Ve-ein meḥashvin'). However, concerning money matters connected to a mitzva – when necessary it is permitted to hold a meeting. And although sometimes dealing with this is heated, since the purpose is sacred, when necessary they were lenient about it. Therefore, people are accustomed to be lenient to sell aliyot in the synagogue for its upkeep, and likewise when there is no other suitable place, it is permitted to hold a meeting in the synagogue for the purpose of a fundraising appeal for the poor or for the upkeep of a yeshiva (Shulḥan Arukh 151:1). And likewise in a pressing situation it is permitted to sell sacred books or the four species in the synagogue, when without this there would be people who would not buy them (Rav Pe'alim part 2, Oraḥ Ḥayim 24).

Scientific lectures, although they have value, since they deal with secular matters, may not be held in the synagogue and the study hall. Only in a pressing situation, in communities where there is a need to bring those who are distant closer and to keep those who are close from drifting away, when there is no other place in which the community can be gathered apart from the synagogue – it is permitted to hold lectures in the synagogue on matters of science, health and economics, similar to what they permitted in feeding guests in the synagogue (Taz 151:1, following the Ramban and those who hold like him regarding a stipulation; Biur Halakha 11, s.v. 'Aval be-yishuvo'). And it is right that they take care to open the lectures with words of Torah, so that the words of science and the advice for life will be a continuation of the words of Torah. When the scientific lecture is intended to explain the Torah, it is permitted from the outset to hold it in the study hall.9

notes_en.en:
Public meetings: in the Biur Halakha (151:1, s.v. 'Ve-ein meḥashvin') he wrote that even if the community needs those calculations and they have no other place, they should not be done in the synagogue, because they are considered levity. And in Responsa Da'at Sofer (Oraḥ Ḥayim 21) he wrote that although in public meetings people deal with mitzva matters, they are drawn into dealing also with secular matters and levity. And in the Ben Ish Ḥai (Vayikra 4) he wrote that it is not fitting to hold public meetings in the synagogue, and even a meeting of "individuals of the community for the improvement of the town" is better held elsewhere, "for in a meeting one will not escape speaking idle and extraneous words". In contrast, in Benei Tziyon (Lichtman 151:11) he wrote that in many places people were accustomed to be lenient to gather "in the synagogue to discuss the affairs of the town", and explained that communal needs are considered mitzva needs, and it is permitted to hold them in the synagogue just as calculations for a mitzva are permitted. And he proved it from the Gemara, Shabbat (150a): "And one goes to synagogues to see to communal affairs on Shabbat", which shows that it is permitted to deal with communal needs in a synagogue, and so the Me'iri wrote there. Until here. And it seems that when the subject is liable to cause tension, it is right not to hold the meeting in the synagogue.
It must further be said, concerning meetings on money matters of a mitzva that were permitted when necessary, that in our day there is generally no need for this, because through the enormous rise in the standard of living we have today many and varied public buildings, and there is no need to gather specifically in the synagogue. Likewise, the permission to hold secular lectures in order to bring those who are distant closer suits very small communities, mainly abroad, that have no other buildings. But when there are other buildings, there is no room to permit it.

sections.title_en: 11. The Women's Section and Annexe Rooms
sections.body_en:
The women's section is included in the synagogue, but since in practice fewer people pray in it and on fewer occasions during the week, people are accustomed to be more lenient with it and to consider its holiness lesser than the holiness of the synagogue. Therefore, on the one hand, since the women's section is included in the synagogue, it is permitted to break the wall between the men's section and the women's section in order to enlarge the women's section at the expense of the men's section, and there is no prohibition of demolishing in a synagogue in this. On the other hand, people are accustomed to be more lenient with it, and therefore even in synagogues where people are accustomed to be stringent not to hold large mitzva meals, when necessary they may be held in the women's section.10
Synagogues and study halls have various annexe rooms, and their status depends on their designation, and they should be divided into three levels:

a) Annexe rooms intended for holding small minyanim regularly are considered a synagogue in every respect (Mishna Berura 154:3). However, sometimes in the main hall of the synagogue people follow the stringent view, not to hold large mitzva meals in it, and in the room intended for a small minyan they follow the lenient view and hold large mitzva meals; all according to what they were accustomed.

b) Annexe rooms intended to serve as classrooms for Torah lessons, in which prayers are held when necessary – from the outset they should be treated with the law of a study hall; but when necessary it is permitted to hold in them lessons in sciences and languages, for this involves a mitzva need, since by studying them they will be able to earn a living when they grow up. And if from the beginning they intended to hold in the classrooms also lessons in sciences and languages, it is considered as though 'they stipulated so', and one may be lenient about this from the outset (see above note 7).11

c) Annexe rooms intended from the beginning for holding meals and events and not for prayers and lessons – although they are part of the synagogue building, and sometimes people even pray in them, they have no holiness, and it is permitted to talk in them about money matters and to hold secular gatherings and lectures in them (Maharam Schick, Oraḥ Ḥayim 69).

notes_en.en: Some hold that the women's section has no holiness of a synagogue at all, since prayer with a minyan is not held in it, and therefore it is forbidden to make a window in the wall of a synagogue for the women's section, because of the prohibition of demolishing in a synagogue (Responsa Mahari Enzil 70; Ḥokhmat Adam 86:15). On the other hand, some hold that since women are obligated in prayer, and come to pray with the men, the women's section has the law of the holiness of a synagogue (Sho'el U-Meshiv, first edition 2:22; Ḥesed Le-Avraham, first edition 14; Yeshu'ot Malko, Oraḥ Ḥayim 11; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 154:7; Mikveh Ha-Mayim 4, Oraḥ Ḥayim 19). And many hold an intermediate view, according to which the women's section has holiness, but it is lesser than that of the main synagogue (Rashak, Peret Ve-Olelot 1; Divrei Ḥayim, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:13; Ḥelkat Yo'av, first edition, Oraḥ Ḥayim 4; Arugat Ha-Bosem, Oraḥ Ḥayim 27; Imrei Yosher 2:12; Rav Alter Shapira there; Teshurat Shai, first edition 27; Torat Ḥesed of Lublin, Oraḥ Ḥayim 4; Sha'arei De'a 12; Tzur Ya'akov 1:152; Rav Herzog, Piskei U-Khetavim part 1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 24; Mayim Ḥayim of R. Ḥayim David Ha-Levi 3:15).

Annexe rooms intended for Torah study, and likewise classrooms in yeshivot, are considered a study hall. Therefore some forbade teaching sciences and languages in them. So wrote Responsa Va-Yomer Yitzḥak (Yoreh De'ah 99), Rav Pe'alim (part 2, Oraḥ Ḥayim 22), Yaskil Avdi (part 1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 7) and Beit Barukh (17:106). However, Rav Hai Gaon permitted teaching children languages and arithmetic in the synagogue in the course of the sacred studies learned there (Otzar Ha-Geonim, Megilla 181). And in the Tzitz Eliezer (9:15) he explained that the permission is in the study hall and not in the synagogue, because the study hall is considered the house of the students. And so wrote Yabi'a Omer (part 7, Oraḥ Ḥayim 21), and testified that in the Porat Yosef yeshiva "teachers of arithmetic and writing would teach in the classrooms in which they studied sacred studies all day" (whose law is like a study hall), and when there is no other place it is permitted because of neglect of Torah study, and he reinforced his words from further poskim.

sections.body_en:
At the time of the funeral one does not bring the bier of the deceased into the synagogue in order to eulogise him. Only if the deceased is a great Torah scholar, "an eminent sage and gaon", are people accustomed to bring his bier into the study hall in which he used to expound, and to eulogise him there (Ramban in the name of a Gaon; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 151:1; Yoreh De'ah 344:20). Some say that people act so only towards the great men of the generations, such as the Gaon of Vilna, who was one of the greatest of the generations (Ḥokhmat Adam 155:18), and Rav Azriel Hildesheimer, who was unique in his generation in Torah and piety (Melamed Le-Ho'il, Yoreh De'ah 106). And some say that one may act so with any great Torah scholar who disseminates Torah to the public in his place, for he is considered "an eminent sage and gaon" in his town (Ḥayim Be-Yad 105, of R. Ḥayim Palagi; Torat Ḥayim of Sofer 151:6; Yabi'a Omer part 7, Yoreh De'ah 31). And so they did in the Merkaz Ha-Rav yeshiva, where they brought the bier of the head of the yeshiva, my teacher and master Rav Shaul Yisraeli, of blessed memory, into the hall of the yeshiva to eulogise him.

A eulogy held not at the time of the funeral, such as at the end of the shiva or the sheloshim: if it is a eulogy whose main content is lamentation and weeping, as was customary in the past, the Sages permitted holding it only on condition that many people take part in it (Megilla 28b), such as when a Torah scholar takes part in it and as a result many people come to take part with him in the eulogy. But if many people do not take part in it, it is not respectful to hold it in the synagogue (Rabbi Avraham Min Ha-Har; Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, Toledot Adam Ve-Ḥava 3:8; Shulḥan Gavoha, Yoreh De'ah 344:2).

But if the main part of the eulogy is based on words of Torah and moral awakening in light of the legacy of the deceased, even when few take part in it, it is permitted to hold it in the synagogue, because it is included in words of Torah and moral instruction for which the synagogue is intended (Rosh Yosef, Megilla 28b; Rav Moshe Pardo, as brought in Ta'alumot Lev 3:17; Yabi'a Omer part 10, Oraḥ Ḥayim 55).

sections.title_en: 13. May One Enter a Synagogue with a Guide Dog?
sections.body_en:
As a rule, bringing animals into the synagogue affronts its honour. In addition, the animals are liable to distract the worshippers. However, about a hundred years ago a way was found to help the blind by means of trained guide dogs. At first only a few made use of guide dogs, and about fifty years ago their use had already become widespread in the USA, and about fifteen years after that in Israel too. About twenty-five years ago (around 5760, 2000), people began to make use of dogs also for those suffering from post-traumatic stress (PTSD), which give them a sense of security and relief from anxiety, and enable them to return to normal functioning. These dogs are trained to sense the anxiety as it begins to creep into the hearts of the sufferers, or when a nightmare begins, and they learn to approach the patient with affection and warmth and calm him. The question is whether a blind person or a trauma sufferer may enter the synagogue with his dog.

Already about seventy years ago in the USA (5713, 1953), Rav Moshe Feinstein answered (Igrot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:45) that a blind person may enter the synagogue with his dog, as we find that the Sages permitted (Jerusalem Talmud, Megilla 3:3) one who wishes to study Torah and is on his way with his donkey to enter the study hall with his donkey. Likewise, it is implied that Abaye, when he was a young and orphaned student, would go under the guidance of his nurse with a lamb everywhere, including the study hall (Berakhot 62a). And it is possible that bringing an animal into the synagogue without need is considered disrespect, but for a great need there is no disrespect. Therefore, so that the blind person can take part in communal prayer and the Torah reading, the blind person may enter the synagogue with his dog, and it is good that he sit at the sides of the synagogue in order to minimise the disturbance to the worshippers.

On the other hand, Rav Breisch argued (Ḥelkat Ya'akov, Oraḥ Ḥayim 34, from 5725, 1965) that it is forbidden to bring a guide dog into the synagogue, because bringing it in greatly degrades the synagogue. And the Sages permitted entering with a donkey or a lamb only into a study hall, just as Torah scholars are permitted to eat in it, but not into a synagogue. In addition, there is a concern that the dog will distract the worshippers from prayer, especially the youngsters, and we find that the Sages established halakhot in order to prevent disturbances and distraction from prayer. In addition, in his words, the custom of going about with dogs is characteristic of those who abandon the Torah and is opposed to the spirit of Judaism, and if they agree to bring a dog into the synagogue a serious breach will be created. And so further rabbis ruled, and held that the solution is to tie the dog outside the synagogue, and one of the worshippers should help the blind person in by the hand.

In practice, the view of those who permit seems correct, because when a dog is brought in for the great need of helping a worshipper there is no affront to the honour of the synagogue. And there is also no concern that the dog will significantly disturb the worshippers, for this is a dog trained to be quiet and not to relieve itself at a time not designated for this. And the gabba'im should arrange a place for them near the entrance, in a manner that will hardly disturb the other worshippers.

But in communities in which the worshippers are not accustomed to meet dogs and to be fond of them, bringing the dog into the synagogue is perceived as a desecration of the sacred, and therefore also disturbs the concentration of prayer; there one may rule according to the view of the rabbis who forbade bringing in these dogs. And if possible, it is preferable to educate the public to have compassion on the blind person or the sufferer from post-traumatic stress, and to allow him to bring his dog into the synagogue.12

notes_en.en:
As a rule, those who forbid bringing a dog into the synagogue hold that there is great disrespect in this, as he wrote in Mikveh Ha-Mayim (5:21): "For there is no greater disparagement and disrespect to the house of prayer than this". And so wrote R. Ḥayim David Ha-Levi (Mayim Ḥayim 3:16), and Yalkut Yosef (151:25) in the name of his father Rav Ovadia Yosef. And so wrote before them Ḥelkat Ya'akov (Oraḥ Ḥayim 34), Rav Kasher (Torah Shelema 15, in the appendices, section 10, in the note), Sha'arim Metzuyanim Ba-Halakha (13:2), Sha'arei Moshe (151:1, of Rav Steinberg of Kiryat Yam) and Mishnat Yosef (9:53). And Rav Amar inclined to this (Shema Shlomo 4:3). And they proposed that the dog be tied outside the synagogue and one of the worshippers guide the blind person on his way inside the synagogue.
However, those who permit hold that there is no great disrespect in this, both because it is customary today to raise pet dogs for enjoyment and to house them in homes, and because it is customary to be considerate of people with disabilities, to honour them and to receive them graciously with their dogs. So wrote the Igrot Moshe (Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:45), the Lubavitcher Rebbe (Igrot Kodesh 18, 6936), Rav Mordekhai Eliyahu (Ma'amar Mordekhai part 2, Oraḥ Ḥayim 14), Rav Pinḥas Toledano (Berit Shalom part 1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 16), Rav Elyashiv ('Mi-Nashim Ba-Ohel', p. 125. And see Tziyunei Halakha part 1, p. 40), R. Ḥayim Kanievsky (Da'at Noteh part 1, Prayer 68), and Piskei Shlomo (1, p. 120).
The discussion branched out in several directions, but it seems that the main dispute is about the general attitude to dogs, and whether bringing them into the synagogue is considered great disrespect. This question depends to a great extent on society's assessment of and attitude to guide dogs. According to those who permit, since it is customary today in developed countries to raise dogs as a hobby, and people have even learned to make use of them for therapy and welfare needs, there is no great disrespect in bringing a dog into the synagogue, and it is permitted to bring them in a pressing situation, as it is customary to allow them to be brought also to other important events. In contrast, those who forbid hold that the attitude to dogs has remained as it was customary for many generations – as a despised and repulsive animal (unlike a donkey, for example), and as the Sages said in several places, mainly concerning barking and frightening dogs. Therefore they also argued that the dog will presumably bark and relieve itself, without knowing that these dogs are trained not to bark for no reason, and not to relieve themselves except at the times and places arranged for this. After all this, since there are communities in which bringing a dog into the synagogue is perceived as a very great disparagement and disrespect, it is understandable that there is room to forbid bringing a dog into the synagogue there, despite the great distress this causes the blind person or the sufferer from post-traumatic stress. Nevertheless, if possible, it is preferable that the rabbi educate the congregation to have compassion on the sufferer, and to agree that he enter the synagogue with his dog, for there is no mitzva or virtue in regarding a dog as a despised animal. Apparently, as the years pass and the public is more exposed to the benefit of guide dogs, the dogs are perceived as a more respected animal, and consequently more rabbis permit bringing them into the synagogue.
It is worth noting that sometimes a dog intended for those suffering from post-traumatic stress is not trained to a high level of restraint, and it tends to play with those around it. And then, if even when its owner sits at the back of the synagogue and tries to calm it, it actually disturbs the prayer, it should not be brought into the synagogue.
